Monosyllabic nouns are either high-toned, as in (114a), or low-toned, as in (114b).' (sec. 6.6); High Spread and Fall Simplification (6.3) operate across word boundaries in the phrase.

3505.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Kurmuk is described as a tone language with three underlying tones (H, L, HL) and five surface tones (H, downstepped H, L, LH, HꜜH), with downdrift and downstep; tone is both lexical and grammatical. Stress, accent and prominence are never attributed to Kurmuk anywhere in the phonology.

3506.dflt: antepenult (stated). Light disyllables (no antepenult) are not addressed for modern Burunge; Kießling's Proto-West-Rift reconstruction (§3, p. 8) has "If the word was composed of light syllables only, stress was fixed on the penultimate, if it was a disyllabic word such as *fala 'skin' (16a), otherwise on the antepenultimate".
3506.prule: Default (accent 1 = toneless words, the great majority in Burunge): stress falls on the penultimate syllable if it is heavy (contains a long vowel or a diphthong); otherwise on the antepenultimate. A syllable bearing the marked high tone (accent 2) always attracts stress; in Burunge accent 2 is marginal (a few nominal collective suffixes -óo/-áa/-áy per Endl's 2000 data, onomastic derivation e.g. buuraa 'beer' > Buuráa personal name, and preverbal clitics). Stress is realised as low pitch in all positions.

tn.quote: all Southern Cushitic1 languages have a pitch-accent-system that works on the morphosyntactic level primarily. ... Accent 1 or “neutral tone” which would be left unmarked assigns level low pitch to all syllables in its domain. ... Accent 2 or “marked tone”, on the other hand, assigns prominence which is realised by high pitch fixed on the terminal syllable of a phonological word ... In Burunge and Alagwa it is merely a marginal phenomenon, with the marked tone (accent 2) being restricted to very few categories

Eine nicht bezeichnete Silbe am Anfang ist tief und jede andere nicht mit Tonzeichen versehene indifferent, d. h. (wenigstens an dem Platze) weder ausgesprochen hoch noch tief.
tn.translation: The language of Busá has the so-called musical syllable tone in a clearly recognisable form and probably to as wide an extent as any other genuine West Sudanic language … The main tones are here too marked á = high, a̍ = mid and à = low, and the double tones lying between them: â = high-low, ǎ = low-high. An unmarked syllable at the beginning is low, and every other syllable not given a tone mark is indifferent, i.e. (at least in that position) neither distinctly high nor low.
tn.cite: Funke, E[mil]. 1915. Die Sprache von Busa am Niger. Mitteilungen des Seminars für Orientalische Sprachen an der Königlichen Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität zu Berlin 18, Abt. III (Afrikanische Studien): 52-84.
tn.locator: pp. 55-56, section 'Der Ton'; tone pairs in fn. 1 p. 56
tn.note: 'Musical syllable tone': high, mid, low plus compound high-low and low-high, marked per syllable (katá 'umbrella' vs káta 'navel'); nouns in isolation tend to a 'dynamic accent' on the last syllable. Checked against the source (tone consistency check, 2026-09-23): system level-and-contour -> tone-and-stress (p. 55 'Der Ton'; p. 58 'Abgeleitete Substantive', Anmerkung between e and f); interaction with stress unstated -> independent (p. 58, 'Abgeleitete Substantive', Anmerkung).

3509.tone: Edmiston 1932 Note 2 (same page) reports pairs spelt alike and accented on the same syllable but distinguished by 'a rising inflection' versus 'a falling inflection on the accented syllable' (shuoma 'swine' falling / 'gift' rising; ngata 'woman' / 'inside'; bata 'women' / 'people'), i.e. lexical pitch contrasts perceived on the accented syllable; she marks no tone in the grammar or dictionary. None of these reports a stress rule, and none denies Edmiston's penultimate prominence.

3511.dq: Wondwosen’s description states that tone in Mositacha is culminative; that is, a lexical word can have at most one prominent syllable; however, tone does not seem to be obligatory. As we will see, some lexical words do not have a syllable that is more prominent than the others. (p. 91; data = 'words in isolation', §6.2 p. 91)
3511.dloc: p. 91 (§6.3 'Tone in Mositacha', opening paragraph); supporting: p. 88 (ch. 6 opening), pp. 89-90 (§6.1), pp. 91-98 (§6.3.1 nouns, ex. 152-160), pp. 99-104 (§6.3.2 verbs, ex. 161-166)
3511.prule: No word-stress rule. Harlow analyses Mositacha as a (restricted) tone language: lexical words in isolation show three contrastive surface pitch patterns, HL (most common: ɗete [42] 'squirrel', luʃa [42] 'leg'; trisyllabic punita [442] 'coffee', 'the second tone is always on the last syllable' p. 98), LH (ʔaʃo [24] 'ancestor'; horokʼe [224] 'hippopotamus') and level (koho [44]/[22] 'ram'; kʼetʃine [444] 'giraffe'). The position of the pitch peak is not predictable from syllable count or weight (the same three patterns recur on CVCV, CVCCV, CVVCV and CVCVCV nouns, exx. 152-160). Prominence is culminative (at most one prominent syllable per lexical word) but not obligatory (level-pitch words have none), so by Hyman's (2009) criteria, which Harlow adopts (pp. 89-90), the language is not a stress language.

3511.tone: Harlow (p. 88): 'Instead of using the term pitch-accent to describe tone in Mositacha, I suggest that Hyman’s term restricted tone language is more helpful'; §6.2 (p. 91): 'Mositacha is a tone language because there are constrastive lexical pitches in comparable environment, albeit it is most likely a restricted tone language.' Two contrastive pitch levels (H, L) established on nouns of identical profile in isolation (ex. 152); no true minimal pairs (fn. 20, p. 92); underlying tones undetermined. The only prominence statement is negative: culminative but not obligatory (p. 91). The primary grammar Wondwosen Tesfaye 2015 (not opened) is reported at p. 91 to call the language 'tone-accent' with exactly one H per lexical word and non-contrastive H/L, i.e. a pitch-accent reading; Harlow rejects that analysis. The word 'stress' is applied to Mositacha only once and untheorised: 'the phonetic realization of word-final, unstressed vowels' (§3.5 Voiceless Vowels, p. 56, ex. 60: /helitta/ [hélíttḁ] 'young man', /punita/ [púnítḁ] 'coffee'), where the devoiced final vowel is called unstressed and the acute marks are placed on the preceding high-pitched syllables; no stress position or rule is ever given. Either way (Harlow's restricted tone, Wondwosen's tone-accent) the verdict is tone or pitch accent.

3515.qtr: 2.3. The tones of Bu. Like most African languages, Bu is a tone language. Indeed, tone plays a very distinctive role in this language, in the sense that a change of tone can bring about a change of meaning: it therefore has lexical value. Tone is the relative pitch of a vocal sound. This implies that tone is contrastive, since the sounds are produced at different pitches. In Bu, pitch is likewise contrastive, as the following examples show: (10) a. jɛ̀n 'tail' b. jɛ́n 'chicken' a. tà 'only' b. tá 'father' a. dʒí 'chin' b. dʒì 'truth/path'. 3516.quote: Tone in Buwal functions at the level of the syllable. ... Buwal has three underlying level tones, low (L), mid (M) and high (H). All three levels are found on nouns, adjectives and adverbs. Verbs, on the other hand, may only carry either low or mid tone. ... In some Chadic languages metrical structure interacts with the tonal system in terms of tone placement. The metrical structure involved is not stress (as normally understood in terms of higher pitch or intensity) but has to do with syllable weight. ... However in Buwal, it seems there is no interaction between metrical structure and tone …

3516.tone: Buwal is described as a three-level tone language (L, M, H); tone is assigned per syllable (not per foot or per word), shown by /HLL/ vs /HHL/ and /LMM/ vs /LLM/ melodies on trisyllabic noun roots; lexical minimal pairs (làm 'help' / lām 'build'; vàn 'family' / vān 'rain') and grammatical tone (imperfective ka- mid vs perfective ka- high). The word 'stress' occurs once in the whole thesis (p. 87), in a definitional aside contrasting Kera-type weight-based metrical structure with stress 'as normally understood in terms of higher pitch or intensity'; the author then reports no metrical (foot/weight) interaction with tone in Buwal (pp. 88, 94). Depressor consonants lower the tone of epenthetic vowels and of mid-tone verbal prefixes (p. 87). Phrase level: utterance-final low boundary tone and a high continuation boundary tone before a pause (§2.7.2.1). No sentence of the form 'Buwal has no stress' exists; the grammar is simply silent on word stress while describing tone in full.

3523.prule: No stress rule is stated for Cat Gia Roglai. 3524.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Every syllable nucleus is associated with one of three tones: low (unmarked), high (acute accent) or falling (grave accent; falling nuclei are always long). High and low tone is determined both lexically and by reconstructable changes: e.g. the past-tense marker hít# is lexically high-toned (Melnar 1998: 30); non-lexical high tone usually results from (i) loss of a following h before two consonants, (ii) loss of a low-tone vowel in the following syllable with a resonant onset, or (iii) backward spread of high tone over resonants (Melnar 1998: 40, Table II-X). 3526.dq: In BZ, monosyllabic words are stressed on the roots with long vowels and short vowels if they are content words. Thus, all monosyllabic words containing either modal or non-modal vowels are stressed if they can stand alone. Particles and prefixes of the form CV are normally unstressed.

3526.heavy: Not a weight rule of record; the author's alternative reading treats phonetically long vowels (lengthened after lenis consonants and under low/falling tone; 'the weight of the nucleus is bimoraic' for long stressed vowels, p. 131) as attracting stress, while stating 'vowel length is not contrastive' (pp. 93, 131).
3526.dflt: (author's length reading) two light syllables -> first syllable stressed
3526.prule: Primary stress is anchored to the lexical root/stem: every content root (monosyllabic or disyllabic) carries primary stress; CV prefixes, particles and clitics are unstressed, and suffixes/clitics attached to a root take only secondary stress. In disyllabic content roots the first (penultimate) syllable is stressed; prefix+root disyllables are final-stressed because the root keeps its stress; in compounds and prefixed polysyllables the final (root) syllable takes primary stress with secondary stress on the penult. The author attributes the placement to phonetic vowel length ('length determines stress'), but states elsewhere that vowel length is not contrastive in BZ.
3526.srule: Affixes and clitic particles attached to a root bear secondary stress while the root keeps primary stress (root+suffix [ˈxàn.ˌtó] 'our boss'; prefix+root [ˌbi.ˈdé] 'does not exist'); in low+falling-tone disyllables (usually compounds) the first syllable has secondary and the falling-tone final syllable primary stress; in polysyllabic forms primary stress is on the ultimate and secondary stress on the penultimate syllable ([lá.ˌbà.ˈdàːʔ] 'huaje').

tn.quote: The Betaza Zapotec tone system consists of four phonological tones: high, low, rising, falling and a phonetic mid tone. ... The list above shows five tones: the high, low, rising and falling tones are contrastive, and the mid tone is the result of tone sandhi. ... BZ has two level tones and two contour tones; in the contour tones, falling and rising tones are formed through two subsequent level tones. The falling tone is formed with a high tone and a low tone (F=HL), and the rising one is formed with a low tone plus a floating high tone (R= L+FHT).
